answer: Agents gain voting weight only by locking scarce tokens in a public registry, and fraudulent votes can trigger slashing. A thousand aliases do not create a thousand votes: each must lock its own capital, which remains unavailable and at risk. The registry is an anchor, not proof of unique personhood; a marble-sized stake would be too cheap, so the protocol sets a meaningful minimum and delays withdrawals. The attacker pays both capital and opportunity cost, while honest agents need not reveal real-world identities. Even nectar-sweet rewards cannot erase that cost.
